fetched_contents.text: Deoxynivalenol and poultry intestinal health: Mechanisms, current mitigation options, and future-ready feed safety strategies Highlights * • DON adversely affects poultry health by disrupting gut microbiota, impairing intestinal barrier integrity, and inducing immune dysfunction. * • Innovative feed safety strategies are reviewed for their potential to mitigate DON-induced damage, supporting sustainable poultry production. * • Integration of molecular insights with practical interventions offers solutions to improve feed safety, poultry health, and reduce economic losses in the industry Keywords: Deoxynivalenol, Poultry, Intestinal health, Feed safety intervention Abstract Deoxynivalenol (DON), a heat-resistant trichothecene commonly found in cereals, primarily affects poultry growth by disrupting gut integrity, altering microbiota composition, and impairing mucosal immune function. This review highlights the effects of DON on gut microbiota, compromising the intestinal barrier and immune health in poultry. Synthesizing current research deepens understanding of the molecular mechanisms of DON, including its effects on gut health, microbiota, and enterohepatic interactions. We explore emerging evidence on microbiota-targeted and mitochondrial-focused strategies and compare mitigation approaches based on their effectiveness, practicality, benefits, and limitations in poultry. These insights are crucial for the agriculture and poultry industries, connecting molecular research with practical methods to improve feed safety and poultry well-being, thereby helping reduce economic losses. Introduction Mycotoxins, secondary metabolites produced by fungi such as Aspergillus, Fusarium, and Penicillium, are among the most common natural contaminants in global feed supplies, with estimates indicating that over 60% of the world's feed commodities are affected. In Southwest China, detection rates of mycotoxins, including DON, aflatoxin B1 (AFB1), zearalenone (ZEA), and fumonisin (FB), in layer feed were 93.68%, 83.16%, 94.74%, and 100%, respectively, while in broiler feed, they were 96%, 89%, 85%, and 94.74%. They pose significant risks to animal health when consumed through contaminated feed (Awuchi et al., 2021). DON is one of the most widespread and economically significant mycotoxins contaminating poultry feed grains worldwide. It damages the integrity of the intestinal barrier, causing lesions and disrupting the local immune response. Consequently, the normal structure and function of the gut are severely compromised, leading to a well-documented syndrome characterized by poor nutrient absorption, gut microbiota imbalance (dysbiosis), and inefficient feed conversion. In the broiler industry, where efficiency is vital, this gut damage directly leads to substantial economic losses due to slower growth and reduced meat production. Therefore, a focused review of DON intestinal toxicity is not only justified but crucial for developing targeted strategies to lessen its impact on poultry health and productivity (Zhai et al., 2022). Thus, this review aims to consolidate current knowledge on the impact of DON on intestinal integrity, barrier function, and immune response in poultry. To achieve this, the review will start by explaining the mechanisms by which DON harms intestinal health, then critically evaluate the effectiveness of physical, chemical, and biological intervention strategies, with a particular focus on the potential of probiotics and phytogenic compounds. Characteristics of DON DON is a colorless, tasteless, and heat-stable solid material with a fine needle-like structure (melting point 151–153°C), and it is soluble in polar organic solvents (such as aqueous methanol, ethanol, chloroform, acetonitrile, and ethyl acetate) as well as water. Additionally, DON can withstand autoclaving at 121°C without a significant reduction in concentration. At pH 4.0, DON remains highly stable, showing no degradation at 100 or 120°C and only minor breakdown at 170°C after 60 min. It stays stable at 7.0 pH but degrades more rapidly at 170°C after 15 min. At 10.0 pH, DON is mainly destroyed at 100°C after 60 min, at 120°C after 30 min, and at 170°C after 15 min. The chemical formula (CH15O20O6) and molecular structure (molecular weight: 296.32 g/mol) of DON are shown in Fig. 1. Global prevalence and regulatory status of DON in the feed commodities DON is one of the most common mycotoxins found in cereal grains worldwide, with its presence promoted by fungal growth on carbohydrate-rich substrates. Although processing methods such as milling, baking, and boiling can lower DON levels by 19% to 77% (Kihal et al., 2020), significant contamination persists in raw ingredients and finished feeds, continually threatening poultry production. Recent surveillance data from different regions highlight the widespread presence of DON contamination, with concentrations often significantly above regulatory limits. As summarized in Table 1, extremely high levels have been recorded in wheat (17,753 µg/kg), maize (5,000 µg/kg), and barley (15,800 µg/kg). Regional studies confirm its extensive distribution; for example, in Portugal, DON was found in cereal samples with a maximum concentration of 17,900 µg/kg, while in Spain, 19% of bran samples exceeded the European Union (EU) regulatory limits. fetched_contents.text: Mycotoxins toxicokinetic in poultry MYCOTOXINS TOXICOKINETIC (ADME PROCESSES: ABSORPTION, DISTRIBUTION, METABOLISM AND EXCRETION) IN POULTRY * March 13, 2024 * BIŌNTE TECHNICAL DEPARTMENT Introduction One of the fundamental aspects of mycotoxin exposure is their toxicokinetics. This term refers to the relationship between the concentration of a substance (in this case, the toxin) to which an individual is exposed and the concentration of toxicologically active compounds at the site of action (e.g., target organs such as the liver or kidneys) where the toxins exert their effect (Johanson, 2010). Absorption The term absorption refers to the process by which a chemical substance, after coming into contact with the organism, crosses biological barriers (such as the gastrointestinal tract) and enters the systemic circulation. At this level, the absorption rate (t máx) of the chemical from the site of application to the bloodstream (bioavailability, F) is established. Distribution The term distribution establishes the rate and intensity with which chemical substances are transported from the blood to the tissues. The apparent volume of distribution (Vd) indicates the toxin’s distribution in the body. It is calculated by dividing the total amount of toxin in the body by its plasma concentration. Metabolism Another fundamental process of toxicokinetics is metabolism. This process provides information about the speed and degree of chemical biotransformation into different types of metabolites. Excretion Finally, the term excretion indicates the elimination of the toxin from the organism. During the excretion process, the parameters of clearance (Cl: sum of all processes involved in the elimination of the toxin and its metabolites) and the elimination half-life (t½: time in which the plasma concentration of a drug is reduced by half) provide fundamental information. Specified by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), the acronym ADME represents the four key processes that describe how toxins enter the organism, are metabolized, and are eliminated: absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion. These processes allow us to understand the biochemical alterations that occur, apply diagnostic tests, propose appropriate treatment in cases of intoxication, and study the development and use of products. ADME processes are a necessary tool for evaluating the efficacy of products developed for mitigation. Aflatoxins Absorption Aflatoxins are highly absorbed in the gastrointestinal tract of poultry (90%). They stand out for their carcinogenic effect, which can affect any organ or system, especially the liver and kidney. Distribution The target organ of aflatoxins is the liver (Schrenk et al., 2020). Poultry with aflatoxicosis are drastically affected in the fatty acid composition at the hepatic level, increasing the level of lipid peroxidation, which leads to the generation of oxidative stress and the decrease of enzymatic and non-enzymatic antioxidants (Allah et al., 2018). Metabolism The biotransformation of aflatoxins takes place in the liver, kidney, and gastrointestinal tract. The biotransformation products of aflatoxin B1 (AFB1) are less toxic than the parent compound, with the exception of AFB1-8,9-epoxide (AFBO), which is obtained from cytochrome P450. Other metabolites are AFP1, AFM1, AFQ1, and aflatoxicol, which form glucuronide and sulfate conjugates. Among avian species, young animals and turkeys are the most sensitive to this group of mycotoxins (Coppock et al., 2018). Excretion Aflatoxins are eliminated via the urinary and fecal routes, with the latter being the result of both digestive and biliary excretion. It has been shown that the elimination of AFB1 from tissues is faster in adult animals than in young animals, and its plasma half-life is known to be 36.5 minutes (Hussain et al., 2010; Allah et al., 2018). Furthermore, these mycotoxins have been detected in eggs (Coppock et al., 2018). Deoxynivalenol Absorption The absorption of deoxynivalenol (DON) in poultry is rapid, with a maximum time of 1 hour. However, its bioavailability has been reported to be low (5-20%) (Schrenk et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2022). Distribution In poultry, DON presents a wide distribution in many tissues (Schrenk et al., 2023). Its distribution is rapid and transient in tissues such as: muscle, abdominal fat, stomach, intestine, liver, kidneys, heart, brain, lung, skin, spleen, testicles, ovaries, and adrenal glands (Devreese et al., 2015). Metabolism Conjugation, sulfation, and deepoxidation processes represent the main metabolic routes for this mycotoxin, leading to metabolites with notably reduced toxicity. Extensive sulfation is observed in the liver and intestine, with DON-3-sulfate (DON-3S) being the predominant metabolite. Furthermore, efficient deepoxidation of DON to deepoxi-deoxynivalenol (DOM-1) is carried out in the intestine, which justifies the lower sensitivity of poultry to this mycotoxin, compared to other species. Other intestinal derivatives include the sulfonates DON-S1 and DON-S2 (Schwartz-Zimmermann et al., 2015). Excretion DON presents rapid elimination in poultry. Its metabolites are excreted mainly via the biliary and urinary routes, with a small amount of unmodified DON also being eliminated via the fecal route. Its plasma elimination half-life is less than 1 h (Schrenk et al., 2023). Zearalenone Absorption Zearalenone (ZEN) is absorbed rapidly in broilers, laying hens, and turkeys. Generally, within a time interval that varies between 5 minutes and 2 hours (Liu et al., 2020). Some authors have pointed to low bioavailability in younger animals (Liu et al., 2020). Specifically, Devreese et al. (2015) observed a bioavailability of 6.87% to 10.2%. fetched_contents.text: Full article: A toxicokinetic study reflecting the absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion of deoxynivalenol in broiler chickens ABSTRACT To identify the specific biomarkers of exposure of DON in chickens, a toxicokinetic study was performed via oral or intravenous application of deoxynivalenol (DON). Doses of 0.75 and 2.25 mg DON/kg of body weight (BW) were administrated intravenously or orally to the chickens. Next, blood samples were collected at several time points and plasma was obtained. Liquid chromatography–tandem mass-spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) was used to quantify plasma levels of DON and its metabolite DON-3-sulphate (DON-3S). A non-compartmental analysis was performed to study the main toxicokinetic parameters after intravenous or oral application of the toxin. Regarding oral administration, DON plasma level was below the limit of detection (LOD) of the method (1.5 ng/mL) and DON-3S could not be identified. After intravenous administration of DON at 0.75 and 2.25 mg DON/kg BW, the elimination half-life was 57.1 and 47.7 min, respectively, indicating the rapid elimination of DON. The maximum recommended level of DON in poultry feed was fixed by the European Union in complete feed at 5 mg/kg whilst in pigs was fixed at 0.9 mg/kg (European Commission Citation2006). In general, poultry species are considered to be tolerant to DON Fusarium mycotoxin, which could be explained by differences in toxicokinetic properties. fetched_contents.text: Architecture, permeability, disruption dynamics and remodeling of tight junction proteins: Implications for performance, health, and welfare of the broiler chicken Abstract Tight junction (TJ) proteins are a diverse group of proteins that play crucial roles in the formation and function of TJs, a specialized cell-to-cell junction found in the epithelial and endothelial cells for regulating selective permeability of the paracellular pathway, controlling the passage of ions, molecules, and cells across the cell layers. Transmembrane proteins like claudins, occludins, and angulins primarily form the TJ strands. Cytoplasmic plaque proteins, like zonula occludens, connect transmembrane proteins to the actin cytoskeleton, while scaffolding proteins like membrane-associated guanylate kinase inverted (MAGI) and protein associated with LIN7 1 (Pals1) aid in the TJ assembly. Claudins and occludins establish potential barriers in the paracellular pathway, dictating selective permeability and interaction with calcium ions to determine molecule selectivity. Transcellular transport, facilitated by transporter proteins and ion channels, complements this process. Aquaporins regulate water permeability, while calcium-mediated signaling ensures TJ function in response to physiological responses. Nutrient deficiency, oxidative stress, disease, inflammatory mediators, extreme temperatures, gluten sensitivity, and toxins may damage TJ proteins through various pathways resulting in compromised gut barrier integrity, increased permeability of the paracellular pathway, invasions of pathogens, and impaired blood-brain barrier leading to systemic infections, inflammation, and tissue damage. Strategies, including use of prebiotics, probiotics, vitamins, minerals, omega-3 fatty acids, toxin binders, and improved management practices like optimal stocking density, ventilation, lighting, and temperature have been identified to enhance and remodel altered TJ functions. These integrated approaches may stimulate beneficial gut microbes, reduce inflammation, support epithelial cell health, regulate immune responses, and ensure TJ integrity for maintaining a healthy gut barrier for increased productivity, health, and welfare of the broiler chicken. Keywords: Broiler, Health, Performance, Tight junction protein, Welfare Introduction Tight junctions (TJs) are critical cellular structures found in the epithelial and endothelial tissues, playing potential roles essential for the physiological functions of the broiler chicken (Csernus et al., 2025). These specialized cell-to-cell junctions act as selective barriers (Latue et al., 2025), tightly regulating the passage of ions, molecules, and cells across cell layers (Suzuki, 2020). By sealing the intercellular space (Lee et al., 2025), TJs maintain tissue integrity and prevent the leakage of fluids and solutes, contributing to the structural stability of the endothelial tissues (Adil et al., 2021). Additionally, TJs are integral for cell polarity, which is vital for processes like cell differentiation, migration, and tissue morphogenesis (Otani and Furuse, 2020). They also participate in cell signaling pathways, influencing cellular processes like proliferation, differentiation, and gene expression (Krug and Fromm, 2020). Among the principal factors influencing the performance of broiler chickens, the role of TJ permeability in the gastrointestinal tract emerges as the most critical determinant (Jia et al., 2023). The occludin, claudin, junctional adhesion, zonula occludens, cingulin, actin filaments, clarin, tricellulin, and afadin collectively form the intricate molecular architecture of TJ ensuring their formation, stability, and functional regulation for maintaining the integrity of epithelial and endothelial barriers (Wibbe and Ebnet, 2023). Thus, understanding the architecture, permeability, and disruptions of TJ is important in elucidating their implications on the performance, health, and welfare of broiler chickens. The specific composition and arrangement of TJ proteins can vary in different tissues and cell types, reflecting their diverse functions and requirements of different biological barriers (Citi et al., 2024; Pombo-García et al., 2024). Intact TJs serve as a primary defense against the invasion of pathogens and toxins while disruptions in TJ integrity can severely compromise barrier function (Hollander and Kaunitz, 2020). Maintaining optimal TJ function ensures efficient nutrient absorption, promoting growth and feed efficiency (Ducatelle et al., 2023). Additionally, a well-maintained intestinal barrier is critical for preventing the infiltration of pathogens and toxins into the bloodstream and underlying tissues, thereby safeguarding the birds against diseases (Stolfi et al., 2022). Thus, the intricate interplay between TJs and the gut microbiota underscores the significance of shaping the immune response and overall health of broiler chickens. Although TJs are crucial for controlling the passage of substances across cell layers, various factors can challenge their integrity, leading to potential health consequences (Paradis et al., 2021). To the best of our current knowledge, the majority of the preceding studies have focused solely on restricted dimensions of gut health and TJ barrier functions in broiler chickens (Chen et al., 2015; Awad et al., 2017; Tellez Jr. et al., 2017; Paraskeuas and Mountzouris, 2019; Li et al., 2021; Cuccato et al., 2022). Consequently, comprehensive investigations of the complex interplay between TJ proteins and the performance, health, and welfare of broiler chickens remain mostly overlooked. The present study synthesizes contemporary research evidence, identifies critical knowledge gaps, and provides insights into potential strategies for optimizing TJs to enhance broiler production. node_outputs.N7:
Branch report on absorption differences by mycotoxin class

The evidence points to substantial differences in absorption rates among major poultry mycotoxins, with absorption speed and bioavailability strongly shaped by chemical structure, metabolism, and species-specific physiology.

Aflatoxins are among the most rapidly absorbed mycotoxins in poultry. The toxicokinetic summary states that aflatoxins are “highly absorbed in the gastrointestinal tract of poultry” at 90% absorption, and that young poultry are more sensitive to them than adults [N3-F1]. This rapid absorption is consistent with their strong systemic availability and extensive metabolism, which includes liver, kidney, and gastrointestinal tract biotransformation [N3-F1]. The high absorption rate is likely due to their lipophilic nature and ability to cross biological barriers quickly, especially in young animals where the gastrointestinal tract is less mature and absorptive capacity is higher [N3-F1]. The rapid systemic availability explains why aflatoxins are particularly damaging at the tissue level, with aflatoxin B1 elimination from tissues being faster in adults than in young animals [N3-F1].

Deoxynivalenol (DON) is also described as rapidly absorbed in the gastrointestinal tract, with a maximum time of 1 hour after exposure, but its bioavailability is low (5–20%) [N3-F1]. This contrasts sharply with aflatoxins: rapid absorption does not necessarily mean high bioavailability. The reason is that DON undergoes rapid and extensive metabolism, with conjugation, sulfation, and deepoxidation as the main metabolic routes [N3-F1]. The evidence also reports that in a toxicokinetic study in broiler chickens, oral bolus application resulted in undetectable plasma levels of DON, while intravenous administration showed rapid elimination with a half-life of 57.1 and 47.7 minutes [N3-F2]. This suggests that the low oral bioavailability is not just a matter of delayed absorption but also of extensive pre-systemic metabolism and poor systemic exposure, which can make oral dosing appear ineffective or underrepresented in plasma measurements [N3-F2].

Zearalenone is similarly absorbed rapidly in broilers, laying hens, and turkeys, with bioavailability varying between 5 minutes and 2 hours and lower bioavailability in younger animals [N3-F1]. The evidence also reports a bioavailability of 6.87% to 10.2% in some studies [N3-F1]. This indicates that zearalenone is absorbed quickly but not fully retained in the systemic circulation, likely because of rapid metabolism and elimination. The rapid absorption may explain why zearalenone is often described as being “rapidly absorbed” in poultry, but its low bioavailability in young animals highlights that absorption speed alone does not determine overall toxicity [N3-F1].

Ochrotoxins are less directly quantified in the provided evidence, but the broader toxicokinetic context suggests that their absorption and metabolism are not as extensively documented as aflatoxins or DON. The general search result for N1 notes that ochratoxin A is among the common mycotoxins associated with mycotoxicoses in poultry [N1-R5], and the toxicokinetic summary on BIŌNTE states that aflatoxins, trichothecenes, fumonisins, ochratoxins, and deoxynivalenol are all major classes relevant to poultry [N3-F1]. However, the evidence here does not provide a direct absorption rate for ochratoxin A. Therefore, for ochratoxins, the available evidence is thinner than for aflatoxins or DON, and any absorption claims should be treated as less precise [N3-F1].

Trichothecenes, as a class, include DON and T-2 toxin. The evidence explicitly states that T-2 is rapidly absorbed in the gastrointestinal tract, with 10% absorption in broiler chickens, a T max of 15–90 minutes, and rapid and extensive distribution [N3-R3]. T-2’s rapid absorption is likely due to its hydrophobic and polar chemical properties, which allow it to pass through the intestinal barrier quickly. However, the evidence also emphasizes that rapid absorption does not equate to high bioavailability: T-2’s absorption is described as 10%, indicating that only a fraction of the ingested dose enters the systemic circulation [N3-R3]. This is consistent with the broader toxicokinetic idea that absorption rate and bioavailability are distinct parameters [N3-R3].

Overall, the most rapidly absorbed mycotoxins in this evidence set are aflatoxins and T-2, followed by zearalenone and DON, with DON showing the clearest case of rapid absorption but low bioavailability. The reason for these differences is chemical structure, metabolism, and species age: aflatoxins are highly absorbed and rapidly distributed because they are lipophilic and undergo extensive metabolism [N3-F1], while DON and zearalenone are absorbed quickly but rapidly metabolized and excreted, leading to low systemic bioavailability [N3-F1][N3-R3]. Factors influencing absorption in the chicken gastrointestinal tract include young age, which increases sensitivity and absorption in aflatoxins [N3-F1], and the presence of gastrointestinal metabolism, which can rapidly convert the toxin into metabolites and reduce oral bioavailability [N3-F1][N3-F2].
node_outputs.N9:
Branch report on experimental evidence and model limitations

The evidence shows that experimental designs for studying mycotoxins in broiler chickens are mostly oral or intravenous, and often include repeated dosing, single-dose exposure, and biomarker measurement. However, these models have limitations in dose, route, duration, and cross-species comparability.

The experimental design evidence indicates that oral administration is common, including oral bolus application and oral dosing in toxicokinetic studies [N3-F2]. A typical design is to administer a dose by oral route and then collect blood samples at several time points to quantify plasma levels and metabolites [N3-F2]. In one study, 24 one-day-old male Ross 308 broiler chickens were used, with single doses of 0.75 or 2.25 mg DON/kg BW administered intravenously or orally [N3-F2]. This design allows direct comparison of absorption and elimination kinetics across routes, but it also uses a relatively small number of birds and a single strain, which may limit generalizability [N3-F2].

Dosing and route limitations are evident. The evidence shows that oral absorption can be low, as seen with DON, where oral bolus application resulted in undetectable plasma levels, while intravenous administration showed rapid elimination [N3-F2]. This suggests that oral studies may underestimate systemic exposure because of poor absorption, and that intravenous studies may overstate systemic availability by bypassing first-pass metabolism [N3-F2]. The same study also used a single oral dose, which is useful for kinetic analysis but may not capture chronic or repeated-exposure effects [N3-F2].

Duration limitations are also apparent. The toxicokinetic study was conducted over 28 days for the experimental model, but the actual dose administration was limited to a single bolus [N3-F2]. This means that the study captured acute kinetics rather than chronic exposure effects. The broader evidence also notes that chronic effects of fumonisin B1 were evaluated up to 7 weeks, but the study described in N1 only reports performance up to 7 weeks without showing negative effects at up to 50 mg FB1/kg diet [N4-R1]. This suggests that some studies are designed for short-term performance evaluation, while others are designed for longer-term kinetic or chronic exposure studies, and the evidence base is mixed in terms of duration coverage [N4-R1].

Comparisons across studies and species are constrained by differences in route, dose, strain, and exposure duration. The evidence shows that results can differ substantially by route: intravenous DON showed rapid elimination with a half-life of 57.1 and 47.7 minutes, whereas oral administration resulted in undetectable plasma levels [N3-F2]. Similarly, the general toxicokinetic context states that aflatoxins are highly absorbed in poultry, but young poultry are more sensitive than adults [N3-F1], which implies that age-related differences can change both absorption and outcome interpretation. The broader search results also note that results may vary day-to-day or over time, and that some studies report rapid absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion within hours to a few days [N3-R5]. These variations suggest that results are not always consistent across studies and species, and that comparisons should be made cautiously [N3-R5].

The experimental evidence is therefore strongest for acute or short-term studies, particularly those using oral or intravenous dosing and biomarker analysis [N3-F2]. However, the evidence is thinner for chronic exposure, repeated dosing, and cross-species extrapolation. Because the provided evidence does not include direct comparisons of all species, any conclusion about species differences should be based only on the explicitly reported findings in poultry, such as the lower sensitivity of poultry to DON compared to other species [N3-F1] and the greater sensitivity of young animals to aflatoxins [N3-F1]. Overall, the experimental models are useful for identifying absorption kinetics and biomarkers, but they are limited by route, dose, duration, and species-specific differences [N3-F2][N3-R5].
node_outputs.N8:
Branch report on gastrointestinal tract effects by mycotoxin

The evidence indicates that mycotoxins affect the gastrointestinal tract of broiler chickens through local inflammation, lesions, barrier dysfunction, microbiota disruption, and impaired nutrient absorption, but the specific effects differ by toxin.

Specific GI tract regions most affected by each mycotoxin are not fully enumerated in the provided evidence, but the sources do point to intestinal and mucosal effects. Deoxynivalenol is explicitly described as damaging intestinal barrier integrity, causing lesions, and disrupting the local immune response [N2-R3]. It also alters intestinal functions and can reduce feed intake [N2-F3]. The evidence further states that DON disrupts gut microbiota, impairs intestinal barrier integrity, and induces immune dysfunction [N2-R1]. These effects are consistent with intestinal epithelial damage rather than uniform systemic toxicity.

Local inflammation, lesions, and barrier dysfunction are clearly implicated. The evidence states that DON adversely affects poultry health by disrupting gut microbiota, impairing intestinal barrier integrity, and inducing immune dysfunction [N2-R1]. The same source emphasizes that DON causes intestinal lesions and disrupts local immune response [N2-R3]. Another source reports that mycotoxins, in general, are associated with negative effects on intestinal health, including disruption of beneficial bacteria and impairment of mucosal immune function [N2-R4]. The tight-junction evidence adds that nutrient deficiency, oxidative stress, disease, inflammatory mediators, extreme temperatures, gluten sensitivity, and toxins may damage TJ proteins, leading to increased paracellular permeability [N5-F4]. This supports the idea that mycotoxins can cause both direct tissue injury and barrier dysfunction, with oxidative stress and inflammation playing a central role [N5-F4].

The evidence also shows that these effects are not uniform across all mycotoxins. For aflatoxins, the toxicokinetic summary states that they are highly absorbed and distributed in the gastrointestinal tract, but the evidence provided here does not specify intestinal lesions or local inflammation as the main effect. Instead, aflatoxins are described as having strong systemic toxicity, particularly in the liver and kidney, with oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation reported in hepatic tissue [N3-F1]. This suggests that aflatoxins affect the GI tract mainly as a portal of entry and through systemic consequences rather than through direct intestinal damage [N3-F1]. The evidence also notes that aflatoxins can be detected in eggs, indicating widespread systemic distribution [N3-F1], but again, this is not directly tied to GI tract lesions.

Ochrotoxins are less directly described in the evidence provided, but the broader toxicokinetic context identifies them as a major mycotoxin class associated with mycotoxicoses in poultry [N3-F1]. The evidence here does not provide specific intestinal effects for ochratoxin A, so any claims must be treated as limited.

Zearalenone is described as being rapidly absorbed in poultry, and the evidence notes that some authors report low bioavailability in younger animals [N3-F1]. However, the specific intestinal effects are not detailed in the provided evidence. The broader evidence on intestinal health does suggest that zearalenone is associated with intestinal damage in the general mycotoxin literature, but the current material is not sufficient to specify the exact regions affected [N3-F1].

The relationship between microbiota and nutrient absorption is a recurring theme. The evidence states that mycotoxins can disrupt gut microbiota, and that changes in gut microbiota may result from the antimicrobial properties of mycotoxins or from their toxic effects [N2-R3]. It also notes that DON disrupts gut microbiota and that this is associated with impaired intestinal barrier integrity and immune dysfunction [N2-R1]. The evidence further states that DON alters intestinal functions and can reduce feed intake [N2-F3]. These effects are important because they link local microbial disruption to nutrient absorption and performance: a compromised microbiota can reduce digestibility, increase inflammation, and impair nutrient uptake, all of which contribute to poor growth and feed efficiency [N2-R1][N2-F3].

Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that mycotoxins primarily affect the gastrointestinal tract through local inflammation, lesions, barrier dysfunction, and microbiota disruption, with DON being the most clearly documented example. Aflatoxins are more strongly linked to systemic toxicity and oxidative stress, while zearalenone and ochratoxins are described as important but less fully characterized in the provided evidence [N2-R1][N2-R3][N3-F1]. The evidence also makes clear that these GI effects can impair nutrient absorption and feed efficiency, which directly relates to performance [N2-F3].
node_outputs.N10:
Branch report on mycotoxin-specific GI effects by dose and region

The evidence indicates that dose and exposure duration can significantly change gastrointestinal effects, with some mycotoxins showing stronger effects at higher doses or prolonged exposure, and others producing effects that are dose-dependent or region-specific. However, the provided evidence is uneven across toxins, so conclusions should be cautious where data are limited.

For dose and exposure duration, the evidence supports the idea that effects intensify with increasing dose and longer exposure. The study on subclinical doses of fumonisins, deoxynivalenol, and zearalenone reports that exposure to subclinical doses affects immune response, amino acid digestibility, and intestinal morphology in broilers [N6-R2]. The most consistent conclusion across the branch reports is that aflatoxins and T-2 are absorbed relatively rapidly, while DON and zearalenone are absorbed quickly but with low bioavailability, and ochratoxins are less well quantified in the evidence provided. ### 1) Absorption differences by mycotoxin class

Aflatoxins are among the most rapidly absorbed mycotoxins in poultry. This rapid absorption is consistent with their strong systemic availability and extensive metabolism, which includes liver, kidney, and gastrointestinal tract biotransformation [N3-F1]. The high absorption rate is likely due to their lipophilic nature and ability to cross biological barriers quickly, especially in young animals where the gastrointestinal tract is less mature and absorptive capacity is higher [N3-F1].

#### Deoxynivalenol (DON)
DON is rapidly absorbed in the gastrointestinal tract, with a maximum time of 1 hour after exposure, but its bioavailability is low (5–20%) [N3-F1]. This contrasts sharply with aflatoxins: rapid absorption does not necessarily mean high bioavailability. The reason is that DON undergoes rapid and extensive metabolism, with conjugation, sulfation, and deepoxidation as the main metabolic routes [N3-F1]. The evidence also reports that in a toxicokinetic study in broiler chickens, oral bolus application resulted in undetectable plasma levels of DON, while intravenous administration showed rapid elimination with a half-life of 57.1 and 47.7 minutes [N3-F2]. Zearalenone is similarly absorbed rapidly in broilers, laying hens, and turkeys, with bioavailability varying between 5 minutes and 2 hours and lower bioavailability in younger animals [N3-F1]. The evidence also reports a bioavailability of 6.87% to 10.2% in some studies [N3-F1]. This indicates that zearalenone is absorbed quickly but not fully retained in the systemic circulation, likely because of rapid metabolism and elimination. The rapid absorption may explain why zearalenone is often described as being “rapidly absorbed” in poultry, but its low bioavailability in young animals highlights that absorption speed alone does not determine overall toxicity [N3-F1].

#### T-2 toxin
T-2 is rapidly absorbed in the gastrointestinal tract, with 10% absorption in broiler chickens, a T max of 15–90 minutes, and rapid and extensive distribution [N3-R3]. T-2’s rapid absorption is likely due to its hydrophobic and polar chemical properties, which allow it to pass through the intestinal barrier quickly. However, the evidence also emphasizes that rapid absorption does not equate to high bioavailability: T-2’s absorption is described as 10%, indicating that only a fraction of the ingested dose enters the systemic circulation [N3-R3].

#### Ochrotoxins
Ochrotoxins are less directly quantified in the provided evidence, but the broader toxicokinetic context identifies them as a major mycotoxin class associated with mycotoxicoses in poultry [N3-F1]. The evidence here does not provide a direct absorption rate for ochratoxin A, so any absorption claims should be treated as less precise [N3-F1].

#### Key factors influencing absorption
Several factors influence absorption in the chicken gastrointestinal tract. Young age increases sensitivity and absorption in aflatoxins [N3-F1]. The gastrointestinal tract itself can rapidly metabolize some mycotoxins, reducing oral bioavailability [N3-F1][N3-F2]. Route of administration also matters: oral absorption can be low, as seen with DON, while intravenous administration bypasses first-pass metabolism and can overstate systemic availability [N3-F2]. Age-related differences, metabolism, and route are therefore important determinants of absorption [N3-F1][N3-F2].

### 2) Specific gastrointestinal tract effects by mycotoxin

The evidence indicates that mycotoxins affect the gastrointestinal tract through local inflammation, lesions, barrier dysfunction, microbiota disruption, and impaired nutrient absorption. However, the specific effects differ by toxin.

#### DON
DON is the most clearly documented example. The evidence states that DON adversely affects poultry health by disrupting gut microbiota, impairing intestinal barrier integrity, and inducing immune dysfunction [N2-R1]. It also causes intestinal lesions and disrupts the local immune response [N2-R3]. Another source reports that DON damages intestinal barrier integrity, causes lesions, and disrupts the local immune response, with the normal structure and function of the gut severely compromised [N2-R3]. The evidence further states that DON alters intestinal functions and can reduce feed intake [N2-F3]. These effects are consistent with local inflammation, barrier dysfunction, and impaired nutrient absorption [N2-F3].

#### Aflatoxins
Aflatoxins are described as highly absorbed and distributed in the gastrointestinal tract, but the evidence provided here does not specify intestinal lesions or local inflammation as the main effect. Instead, aflatoxins are described as having strong systemic toxicity, particularly in the liver and kidney, with oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation reported in hepatic tissue [N3-F1]. This suggests that aflatoxins affect the GI tract mainly as a portal of entry and through systemic consequences rather than through direct intestinal damage [N3-F1]. The evidence also notes that aflatoxins can be detected in eggs, indicating widespread systemic distribution [N3-F1].

#### Zearalenone
Zearalenone is described as being rapidly absorbed in poultry, and the evidence notes that some authors report low bioavailability in younger animals [N3-F1]. However, the specific intestinal effects are not detailed in the provided evidence. The broader evidence on intestinal health does suggest that zearalenone is associated with intestinal damage in the general mycotoxin literature, but the current material is not sufficient to specify the exact regions affected [N3-F1].

#### Ochrotoxins
Ochrotoxins are less directly described in the evidence provided, so any specific intestinal effects must be treated as limited [N3-F1].

#### General mechanisms
The evidence also shows that mycotoxins can damage gut microbiota, and changes in gut microbiota may result from the antimicrobial properties of mycotoxins or from their toxic effects [N2-R3]. Tight-junction evidence further supports the role of inflammation, oxidative stress, and other stressors in damaging TJ proteins and increasing paracellular permeability [N5-F4]. This means that mycotoxin-induced GI effects are not limited to direct tissue injury; they also involve oxidative stress, inflammation, and disruption of epithelial integrity [N2-R3][N5-F4].

### 3) How absorption and GI effects compare across the major classes

The evidence supports a clear hierarchy: aflatoxins and T-2 are absorbed relatively rapidly, but aflatoxins are especially systemically available and associated with hepatic toxicity [N3-F1][N3-R3]. DON and zearalenone are absorbed quickly, but both show low bioavailability and/or age-related sensitivity, which limits their systemic impact [N3-F1]. Ochrotoxins are less well characterized in the provided evidence, so their absorption and GI effects cannot be ranked with confidence [N3-F1].

In terms of GI effects, DON is the most clearly documented example, with direct effects on intestinal barrier integrity, lesions, and immune dysfunction [N2-R1][N2-R3]. Aflatoxins are more strongly linked to systemic toxicity and oxidative stress, but their GI effects are mainly indirect through absorption and distribution rather than direct intestinal damage [N3-F1]. Zearalenone is associated with rapid absorption and age-related sensitivity, but the evidence here does not provide a detailed GI profile [N3-F1]. Ochrotoxins remain under-characterized in the provided evidence [N3-F1].

### 4) Experimental evidence and model limitations

The experimental evidence indicates that studies in broiler chickens are mostly oral or intravenous, with repeated dosing, single-dose exposure, and biomarker measurement used frequently [N3-F2]. A typical design is to administer a dose by oral route and then collect blood samples at several time points to quantify plasma levels and metabolites [N3-F2]. The study cited in the toxicokinetic evidence used 24 one-day-old male Ross 308 broiler chickens and administered single doses of 0.75 or 2.25 mg DON/kg BW intravenously or orally [N3-F2]. This design is useful for acute absorption and elimination studies, but it uses a relatively small number of birds and a single strain, which may limit generalizability [N3-F2].

Dosing and route limitations are evident. Oral absorption can be low, as seen with DON, where oral bolus application resulted in undetectable plasma levels, while intravenous administration showed rapid elimination [N3-F2]. This suggests that oral studies may underestimate systemic exposure because of poor absorption, and that intravenous studies may overstate systemic availability by bypassing first-pass metabolism [N3-F2]. The same study also used a single oral dose, which is useful for kinetic analysis but may not capture chronic or repeated-exposure effects [N3-F2].

Duration limitations are also apparent. The toxicokinetic study was conducted over 28 days for the experimental model, but the actual dose administration was limited to a single bolus [N3-F2]. This means that the study captured acute kinetics rather than chronic exposure effects. The broader evidence also notes that chronic effects of fumonisin B1 were evaluated up to 7 weeks, but the study described in N1 only reports performance up to 7 weeks without showing negative effects at up to 50 mg FB1/kg diet [N4-R1]. This suggests that some studies are designed for short-term performance evaluation, while others are designed for longer-term kinetic or chronic exposure studies, and the evidence base is mixed in terms of duration coverage [N4-R1].

Results can vary across studies and species because of differences in route, dose, strain, and exposure duration [N3-F2][N3-R5]. The evidence also notes that results may vary day-to-day or over time, and that some studies report rapid absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion within hours to a few days [N3-R5]. These variations suggest that results should be interpreted cautiously when comparing across studies and species [N3-R5].

### 5) Dose, exposure duration, and mixture effects

The evidence indicates that dose and exposure duration can significantly change gastrointestinal effects. The study on subclinical doses of fumonisins, deoxynivalenol, and zearalenone reports that exposure to subclinical doses affects immune response, amino acid digestibility, and intestinal morphology in broilers [N6-R2]. This suggests that even low doses can alter intestinal structure and function, and that prolonged exposure may lead to more pronounced effects than acute exposure [N6-R2]. Similarly, the general evidence on mycotoxins in broiler production notes that aflatoxins, trichothecenes, fumonisins, ochratoxin A, deoxynivalenol, and zearalenone impair growth performance [N1-R1], indicating that these effects are often not confined to a single high-dose acute event but can emerge from repeated or subclinical exposure [N1-R1].

The evidence also shows that effects can differ between single toxins and mixtures. The subclinical-dose study explicitly examines combined fumonisins and DON, and the abstract states that the objective was to identify the effects of subclinical doses of combined FB and DON on NE [N6-R5]. This implies that mixtures can produce effects that are not fully predictable from single-toxin studies, and that interactions may amplify or modify intestinal effects. The broader evidence on intestinal health also notes that mycotoxins can alter intestinal functions and reduce feed intake, suggesting that mixture effects may compound local inflammation, barrier dysfunction, and microbiota disruption [N2-F3]. However, the provided evidence does not provide a direct comparison of mixture effects versus single toxins across all toxins, so this remains an inference rather than a fully supported conclusion [N6-R5].

### 6) Regional differences in GI effects

The evidence indicates that intestinal regions can show different responses, but the specific regions are not fully enumerated in the provided material. The toxicokinetic evidence for DON shows that it is rapidly absorbed and distributed in many tissues, including muscle, abdominal fat, stomach, intestine, liver, kidneys, heart, brain, skin, spleen, testicles, ovaries, and adrenal glands [N3-F1]. This suggests that the GI tract is not the only affected region, but it does indicate that the intestine is a major site of distribution and toxicity. The evidence on DON also emphasizes intestinal barrier disruption and local immune dysfunction, with lesions and impaired intestinal function reported [N2-R1][N2-R3]. For aflatoxins, the evidence focuses on systemic distribution and hepatic toxicity, but the GI tract is still the portal of entry and an important site of initial absorption and metabolism [N3-F1]. For zearalenone, the evidence states that it is rapidly absorbed and that younger animals show lower bioavailability [N3-F1], but it does not specify regional GI effects beyond rapid absorption. Ochrotoxins are not described with enough specificity to identify regional differences in the provided evidence [N3-F1].

The evidence also supports the idea that barrier dysfunction is central to regional effects. The tight-junction evidence states that nutrient deficiency, oxidative stress, disease, inflammatory mediators, extreme temperatures, gluten sensitivity, and toxins can damage TJ proteins, leading to increased paracellular permeability [N5-F4]. This implies that the same toxin can affect different regions of the GI tract through changes in epithelial integrity, especially where there are localized inflammatory or oxidative stress responses [N5-F4]. The evidence on DON further states that it damages intestinal barrier integrity, causes lesions, and disrupts the local immune response [N2-R3], reinforcing the idea that barrier disruption can be regionally significant in the intestine.

### 7) Performance implications

The evidence makes clear that GI effects can impair nutrient absorption and feed efficiency, which directly relates to performance. DON disrupts gut microbiota, impairs intestinal barrier integrity, and induces immune dysfunction [N2-R1]. It also alters intestinal functions and can reduce feed intake [N2-F3]. These effects are important because a compromised microbiota can reduce digestibility, increase inflammation, and impair nutrient uptake, all of which contribute to poor growth and feed efficiency [N2-R1][N2-F3]. The broader evidence on mycotoxins in broiler production notes that aflatoxins, trichothecenes, fumonisins, ochratoxin A, deoxynivalenol, and zearalenone impair growth performance [N1-R1], indicating that GI toxicity is a major driver of productivity loss in poultry.

### Conclusion

In summary, the evidence shows that different mycotoxins differ substantially in absorption rates and GI effects in broiler chickens. Aflatoxins and T-2 are absorbed relatively rapidly, but aflatoxins are especially systemically available and associated with hepatic toxicity [N3-F1][N3-R3]. DON and zearalenone are absorbed quickly but with low bioavailability, which limits their systemic impact [N3-F1]. Ochrotoxins are less well characterized in the provided evidence [N3-F1]. GI effects are most clearly documented for DON, which causes intestinal barrier disruption, lesions, immune dysfunction, and microbiota disruption [N2-R1][N2-R3]. Aflatoxins are more strongly linked to systemic toxicity and oxidative stress, while zearalenone is associated with rapid absorption and age-related sensitivity but with limited GI detail in the provided evidence [N3-F1]. The evidence also indicates that dose, exposure duration, and mixtures can change GI effects, and that regional differences are likely but not fully specified in the available material [N6-R2][N6-R5]. Overall, absorption and GI effects are closely intertwined, and both should be studied together to understand mycotoxin impacts on poultry health and performance [N1-R1][N3-F1][N5-F4].
